Field sparrow (Spizella pusilla) embryos develop within eggs incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a temperature that yields a hatching period of 12 days [ab = 12 days]. This incubation duration, typical among small New World sparrows, reflects the thermal optimum for embryonic differentiation within the calcareous egg. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings emerge with a wet weight of 1.2 grams [Wwb = 1.2 grams], a modest mass that underscores their total dependence on parental provisioning during the early nestling phase. The initial wet weight of the newly laid egg itself is 1.71 grams [Ww0 = 1.71 grams], indicating that nearly thirty percent of the egg's initial mass is lost as metabolic water and shell material prior to hatching. This pattern is consistent with the high energetic cost of producing a calcified egg in a species that relies heavily on cryptic nest placement to mitigate predation risk. The relatively short incubation period may also be an adaptation to the ephemeral nature of early successional habitats that this species frequently occupies.

During the nestling stage, which spans the period from hatching to the attainment of flight capability, chicks undergo a dramatic transformation in body mass. Under the typical thermal conditions associated with active metabolic periods in this species, approximately 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], fledging occurs at 7.5 days after hatching [tx = 7.5 days after hatching]. This developmental milestone marks the achievement of sustained flight and the departure from the nest, although post-fledging parental care often continues for an additional period. The ultimate wet weight of adult Field sparrows reaches 12.28 grams [Wwi = 12.28 grams], representing a more than tenfold increase from the neonatal mass. This growth trajectory is typical of small passerines that exhibit a rapid exponential phase of mass gain followed by a plateau as skeletal and muscular development is completed. The asymptotic mass is attained well before the onset of reproductive activity, ensuring that individuals have sufficient somatic reserves to support the high energetic demands of breeding.

Reproductive maturity in Field sparrows is reached after a protracted juvenile phase. The time since birth at puberty is 22.5 days [tp = 22.5 days], measured from the day of hatching, when maintained at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This relatively brief interval to sexual maturation reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproduction in a species occupying ephemeral, disturbance-dependent habitats where adult mortality can be substantial. Following the attainment of puberty, individuals typically defer their first breeding attempt until the subsequent breeding season. The time since birth at first brood is 365 days since birth [tR = 365 days since birth], a delay that corresponds to the interval required for territory acquisition, pair formation, and the accumulation of sufficient body condition to sustain egg production at a temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C]. This delay is common among temperate-zone passerines that breed seasonally and must synchronize nesting with peak invertebrate prey abundance.

Regarding reproductive output, Field sparrows produce clutches consisting of 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 eggs per clutch], a number that is remarkably consistent across their geographic range. Females typically raise approximately 2 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches annually] during the breeding season, with some individuals in southern populations occasionally attempting a third brood under favorable conditions. This reproductive schedule means that a single female can produce up to 8 offspring per year, placing significant energetic demands on both the incubating female and the provisioning male. The maximum lifespan recorded in wild populations, when measured at an active metabolic body temperature of 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C], reaches approximately 10.3 years [am = approximately 10.3 years], although the majority of individuals survive for only one or two breeding seasons due to high predation pressure and the challenges of overwinter survival. This longevity represents the upper bound of the species' potential lifespan under favorable conditions.

Seasonal variation in environmental conditions exerts a strong influence on the timing of life-history events in this species. The initiation of gonadal recrudescence in early spring is cued by photoperiod, and the progression to full reproductive competence requires both adequate fat reserves and sustained access to high-protein arthropod prey. In years with early spring warming, the first clutches may be initiated several days sooner, potentially allowing additional renesting attempts following predation events. The fledging period of 7.5 days [tx = 7.5 days] at 40.5 °C [T = 40.5 °C] is among the shortest recorded for similarly sized emberizids, a trait that may reduce the window of nest vulnerability to predators. Beyond the breeding season, juveniles undergo a complete preformative molt before their first winter, and adults undergo a prebasic molt following the completion of breeding. These molting periods represent additional physiological bottlenecks that compete with reproductive effort for available energy and nutrients, shaping the overall pace of the species' annual cycle.
